title: Sample a range of seed lots

lessons.title: Sampling different seed lots in practice
lessons.html:
Range matters

Seed comes in many sizes, shapes and packages. In this workplace module you sample a range of seed lots under supervision so that you can handle any situation correctly. Your mentor will arrange work across species and container types.

Types of seed you should sample

  • Large, free-flowing seed: maize, soybeans, beans, sunflower; usually stick or Nobbe triers.
  • Small, free-flowing seed: wheat, canola, sorghum, lucerne; triers with suitable slot sizes.
  • Chaffy, non-free-flowing seed: many pasture grasses; hand sampling.
  • Coated, pelleted or treated seed: extra care to avoid damage and exposure.
  • Vegetable seed in small packets or tins.

Types of containers

  • Paper or woven bags stacked on pallets.
  • Mini-bulk bags.
  • Bulk bins or silos, often sampled from the stream during filling or emptying with an automatic sampler.
  • Small sealed containers, where whole containers may be taken as primary samples as the rules allow.

Each time you sample

  1. Confirm species, lot number, lot size and purpose of sampling.
  2. Check the lot is within the maximum size and appears uniform.
  3. Determine the number of primary samples required from the rules.
  4. Choose the right instrument and sample containers spread across the lot.
  5. Form the composite sample and reduce it with an approved method.
  6. Pack, seal and label the submitted sample; complete the sampling report.

Safety

Wear gloves and a dust mask with treated seed and read the treatment label or safety data sheet. Watch forklift movements, never climb unstable stacks, and wash hands before eating or smoking.

Keep your sampling kit clean and complete: triers of different sizes, a clean composite container, divider, sample bags, seals, labels, forms, pens, gloves, mask and hand-wash supplies. Check the kit before each visit, because a missing item can mean a wasted trip.

lessons.title: Recording, problems and evidence
lessons.html:
Your sampling log

Keep a log of every lot you sample: date, client, species, cultivar, lot number, lot size, number and type of containers, number of primary samples, instrument and method, reduction method, seal numbers and any observations. Have your mentor sign entries after observing your work.

Problems you are likely to meet

SituationCorrect response
Containers stacked so only some can be reachedAsk for the lot to be rearranged; do not sample only the outside
Lot number missing on some bagsDo not sample until identity is confirmed
Different treatment colours within the lotSuspect non-uniformity; report and record
Lot larger than the maximum sizeLot must be divided before sampling
Seed bridging in the trierUse a more suitable instrument or hand sampling
Damp or damaged bagsRecord and report; may affect quality and uniformity

Working with clients

Seed company staff may want samples taken quickly. Explain politely that the rules must be followed for the results to be valid, and that a poor sample could lead to an incorrect result that harms them. Remain independent and do not accept samples drawn by others unless the procedure allows it.

Evidence for your portfolio

  • Signed sampling log covering a range of species and container types.
  • Copies of sampling reports.
  • Mentor observation checklists.
  • Notes on problems you dealt with and how.
  • Laboratory feedback where samples were rejected or questioned, with what you changed.

All evidence must be your own work and current.

Key points

  • Sample a range of species, seed types and containers.
  • Choose instruments to suit seed size and flow.
  • Confirm lot identity, size and uniformity before sampling.
  • Record every sampling in a signed log.
  • Stay independent and follow the rules even under time pressure.
